# Understanding Models and Equations {#sec-lecture-02}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/setup.R")
library(gt)
library(gapminder)
library(ggrepel)
library(patchwork)
```

In research outputs, all the sections are linked (@fig-l02-sections).

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-l02-sections
%%| fig-cap: "The sections of a research output are linked."
%%| fig-alt: "Flow chart from left to right with five boxes, Introduction, Literature Review, Methods, Results, and Discussion and Conclusion, each linked to the next by an arrow."
%%| fig-width: 5.7
flowchart LR
  A[Introduction] --> B[Literature<br/>Review]
  B --> C[Methods]
  C --> D[Results]
  D --> E[Discussion &<br/>Conclusion]
```

To understand the statistics in the results section, it is essential to identify the concepts presented in each section: the variables, the hypotheses, the model and equation, and the statistical test (@fig-l02-concepts).

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-l02-concepts
%%| fig-cap: "The concepts to identify between the sections of a research output."
%%| fig-alt: "The same flow chart with a label on each arrow: Variables between Introduction and Literature Review, Hypotheses between Literature Review and Methods, Model and Equation between Methods and Results, and Statistical Test between Results and Discussion and Conclusion."
%%| fig-width: 5.7
flowchart LR
  A[Introduction] -- Variables --> B[Literature<br/>Review]
  B -- Hypotheses --> C[Methods]
  C -- Model &<br/>Equation --> D[Results]
  D -- Statistical<br/>Test--> E[Discussion &<br/>Conclusion]
```

The variables and the hypotheses are the subject of @sec-lecture-01. This chapter is about the next two concepts, the model and the equation. @sec-l02-models shows how to represent the model tested in a paper: the rules to follow, the types of model, what makes a good model and the tools to draw one. @sec-l02-equations explains the equation used to test the hypotheses: its coefficients, the role of the intercept and the ways to write an equation. The chapter ends with the steps to follow from the variables to the equation (@sec-l02-conclusion).

## Model representation in the method section of an academic research paper {#sec-l02-models}

### The method section {#sec-l02-method}

The method section of an academic paper is always structured in the same way:

1. **Observations.** A short section presenting where the data are coming from. If they are coming from human participants, then their average age and gender are indicated.
2. **Variables.** A short section presenting each variable as well as their type and role.
3. **Procedure.** A short section presenting how the data were collected.
4. **Data analytics.** A short section to display how the hypotheses are tested, by displaying a graphical representation of the model and its corresponding equation(s).

The last part, the model and its equation, is the topic of this chapter.

### Rules and notation {#sec-l02-rules}

A **model** is an overview of the predicted relationships between the variables stated in the hypotheses. To represent a model, you must follow four rules:

- **Rule 1**: all the arrows correspond to a hypothesis to be tested.
- **Rule 2**: all the tested hypotheses have to be represented with an arrow.
- **Rule 3**: hypotheses using the same outcome variable should be included in the same model.
- **Rule 4**: only one outcome variable is included in each model (except for SEM models, see @sec-l02-sem).

The arrows have a meaning. A simple arrow is a **main effect** and a crossing arrow is an **interaction effect** (@fig-l02-arrows). By default, an interaction effect involves the test of the main effect hypotheses of all the predictors involved.

::: {#fig-l02-arrows}

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-arrows-main
//| fig-cap: "A simple arrow is a main effect."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Predictor with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Outcome."
//| fig-width: 2.11
//| fig-height: 0.52

digraph {
  rankdir="LR"
  node [shape=box]
  Predictor -> Outcome
}
```

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-arrows-interaction
//| fig-cap: "A crossing arrow is an interaction effect."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Predictor 1 and a box labelled Outcome joined by a horizontal line with an arrowhead at Outcome. A box labelled Predictor 2 has an arrow pointing down to the middle of that line."
//| fig-width: 3.58
//| fig-height: 0.94

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Predictor 1"; "Predictor 2"; "Outcome"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Predictor 2" -> ""
  "Predictor 1" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> Outcome

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Predictor 2"; "";
  }
}
```

The two kinds of arrows of a model.
:::

The shapes also have a meaning. **Squares** are actual **measures** or **items**, whereas **circles** are **latent variables** related to measures or items. For example, $Salary$ is directly measured (in \$, € or £) so it is a square, whereas $Job\,Satisfaction$ is a latent variable with several questions so it is a circle. Items used for latent variables can be omitted in a model, because the variables are the most important.

### Main effects and interaction effects {#sec-l02-effects}

The relationship between one predictor and one outcome variable is represented by a simple arrow (@fig-l02-main). The first model tests one main effect hypothesis. The second model, with two predictors and one outcome variable, tests two main effect hypotheses.

::: {#fig-l02-main}

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-main-one
//| fig-cap: "One predictor and one outcome variable."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Predictor 1 with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Outcome."
//| fig-width: 2.23
//| fig-height: 0.52

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
}
```

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-main-two
//| fig-cap: "Two predictors and one outcome variable."
//| fig-alt: "Two boxes, Predictor 1 and Predictor 2, each with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Outcome."
//| fig-width: 2.23
//| fig-height: 1.16

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

Models with main effects only.
:::

An **interaction** (also called **moderation**) means that the effect of Predictor 1 on the outcome variable will be different according to the possibilities of Predictor 2. It is represented by the crossing arrow of the effects representation in @fig-l02-interaction, which gives exactly the same results as the model where the interaction is a predictor of its own. This model tests three hypotheses: 2 main effects and 1 interaction effect.

::: {#fig-l02-interaction}

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-interaction-effects
//| fig-cap: "Effects representation."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Predictor 1 and a box labelled Outcome joined by a horizontal line with an arrowhead at Outcome. A box labelled Predictor 2 has an arrow pointing down to the middle of that line."
//| fig-width: 3.58
//| fig-height: 0.94

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Predictor 1"; "Predictor 2"; "Outcome"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Predictor 2" -> ""
  "Predictor 1" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> Outcome

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Predictor 2"; "";
  }
}
```

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-interaction-term
//| fig-cap: "Exactly the same results, with the interaction as a predictor of its own."
//| fig-alt: "Three boxes, Predictor 1, Predictor 2 and Predictor 1 X Predictor 2, each with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Outcome."
//| fig-width: 3.16
//| fig-height: 1.79

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 1 X Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

Two equivalent representations of an interaction effect.
:::

### Types of model {#sec-l02-types}

There are three types of model: simple models, mediation models and structural equation models.

#### Simple model

A **simple model** has one or more predictors and only one outcome. It is made of main effects or/and interaction effects. Simple models are the most statistically powerful, easy to test and reliable models. Always prefer a simple model compared to a more complicated solution.

::: {.callout-important title="Warning"}
Including an interaction effect requires a significantly higher sample size.
:::

In the example of @fig-l02-simple, Salary, Gender and Age are the predictors of Job Satisfaction, which is a latent variable and so a circle. Salary and Gender have an interaction effect. This model tests four hypotheses: 3 main effects and 1 interaction effect.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-simple
//| fig-cap: "A simple model with three main effects and one interaction effect."
//| fig-alt: "Three boxes, Salary, Gender and Age, and a circle labelled Job Satisfaction. Age has an arrow to the circle. Salary and the circle are joined by a line with an arrowhead at the circle, and Gender has an arrow pointing down to the middle of that line."
//| fig-width: 3.11
//| fig-height: 1.48

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Salary"; "Gender"; "Age"
  node [shape = circle, width = 1, fixedsize = true]
  "Job\nSatisfaction"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Age" -> "Job\nSatisfaction"
  "Gender" -> ""
  "Salary" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> "Job\nSatisfaction"

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Gender"; "";
  }
  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Age"; "Salary";
  }
}
```

#### Mediation model

A **mediation model** (simple or moderated) has at least 2 predictors, one of them being called the **mediator**, and only one outcome. It is made of main effects only for a simple mediation, and of main and interaction effects for a moderated mediation.

A mediation model is a complex path analysis between 3 variables, where one of them explains the relationship between the other two. It is usually used to identify cognitive processes in psychology. @fig-l02-mediation shows an example with Exam Results, Self-Esteem and Happiness. This model tests one hypothesis, 1 mediation effect, but it requires 2 main effects.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-mediation
//| fig-cap: "A mediation model with Exam Results, Self-Esteem and Happiness."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Exam Results with arrows to two ovals, Self-Esteem and Happiness, and an arrow from Self-Esteem to Happiness."
//| fig-width: 4.63
//| fig-height: 0.79

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]

  node [shape = box]
  "Exam Results"
  node [shape = oval]
  "Self-Esteem"; Happiness

  "Exam Results" -> {Happiness "Self-Esteem"}
  "Self-Esteem" -> Happiness

}
```

#### Structural equation model {#sec-l02-sem}

A **structural equation model** (SEM) has at least 2 predictors (usually latent variables) and one or more outcomes. It is made of main or/and interaction effects. It is a complex path analysis between multiple variables, including multiple outcomes, and using factor analysis for latent variable estimation.

::: {.callout-tip title="Item contribution to a latent variable"}
The relationship between items of a scale and their corresponding latent variable is considered as significant by default if the scale is valid.
:::

In @fig-l02-sem, each latent variable (oval) is measured by its items (boxes). For example, this model tests four hypotheses.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-sem
//| fig-cap: "A structural equation model: latent variables (ovals) measured by items (boxes), and the arrows between the variables."
//| fig-alt: "Three ovals, Perceived Ease-of-use, Perceived Usefulness and Intention to Use, each linked by plain lines to its own boxes: PEOU1 to PEOU4, PU1 to PU5, and BI1 and BI2. Arrows run from Perceived Ease-of-use to Perceived Usefulness and to Intention to Use, from Perceived Usefulness to Intention to Use, and from Intention to Use to a box labelled Actual Use."
//| fig-width: 5.6
//| fig-height: 5.5

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]

  node [shape = oval]
  "Perceived Ease-of-use"; "Perceived Usefulness"; "Intention to Use"

  node [shape = box]
  PU1; PU2; PU3; PU4; PU5; PEOU1; PEOU2; PEOU3; PEOU4; BI1; BI2; "Actual Use"

  {PU1 PU2 PU3 PU4 PU5} -> "Perceived Usefulness" [arrowhead = none]
  {PEOU1 PEOU2 PEOU3 PEOU4} -> "Perceived Ease-of-use" [arrowhead = none]
  {BI1 BI2} -> "Intention to Use" [arrowhead = none]

  "Perceived Usefulness" -> "Intention to Use"
  "Perceived Ease-of-use" -> {"Perceived Usefulness" "Intention to Use"}
  "Intention to Use" -> "Actual Use"

  subgraph {
      rank = same; "Perceived Usefulness"; "Perceived Ease-of-use";
  }

  subgraph {
      rank = same; PU1; PU2; PU3; PU4; PU5; PEOU1; PEOU2; PEOU3; PEOU4; BI1; BI2;
  }

}
```

### What makes a good model {#sec-l02-good}

A good model has the following qualities:

- **Comprehensiveness**: explains a wide range of phenomena.
- **Internal consistency**: propositions and assumptions are consistent and fit together in a coherent manner.
- **Parsimony**: contains only those concepts and assumptions essential for the explanation of a phenomenon.
- **Testability**: concepts and relational statements are precise.
- **Empirical validity**: holds up when tested in the real world.

@fig-l02-good gives an example of a good model: it is the model of @fig-l02-sem without the items of the scales.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-good
//| fig-cap: "An example of a good model, without the items of the scales."
//| fig-alt: "Three ovals and a box. Perceived Ease-of-use has arrows to Perceived Usefulness and to Intention to Use, Perceived Usefulness has an arrow to Intention to Use, and Intention to Use has an arrow to a box labelled Actual Use."
//| fig-width: 5.6
//| fig-height: 1.1

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]

  node [shape = oval]
  "Perceived Ease-of-use"; "Perceived Usefulness"; "Intention to Use"

  node [shape = box]
  "Actual Use"

  "Perceived Usefulness" -> "Intention to Use"
  "Perceived Ease-of-use" -> {"Perceived Usefulness" "Intention to Use"}
  "Intention to Use" -> "Actual Use"

  subgraph {
      rank = same; "Perceived Usefulness"; "Perceived Ease-of-use";
  }
}
```

On the contrary, a bad theory or model is too complicated, does not explain many things and cannot be tested.

### Drawing a model {#sec-l02-drawing}

The representation of a model can easily be done directly in a manuscript written with Microsoft Word. For more details, it is also possible to draw the model in Microsoft PowerPoint and to copy-paste it in Microsoft Word.

::: {.callout-important title="Warning"}
- Do NOT fill boxes with any colour, use only black and white.
- Use line arrows, no thick arrows allowed.
:::

Besides MS Word and PowerPoint, there are some ways to draw models in a nicer way.

**Flowchart software and websites.** There are many of them and Google would find them very quickly but, to my knowledge, <https://www.diagrams.net/> is free, easy to use and very efficient.

**Flowchart coding languages.** Going further into the details of how to design academic models, flowchart coding languages are the ultimate step. Instead of using a GUI, it is possible to draw models from a couple of lines of code, which is faster after practising a lot. To my knowledge, the main flowchart coding language tools implementing the [DOT style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOT_(graph_description_language)) are: <!-- check: the slide lists mermaid-js, viz-js and nomnoml as DOT style tools; as far as I know only viz-js reads DOT, while mermaid and nomnoml have their own syntax -->

- [mermaid-js](http://mermaid-js.github.io/mermaid/##/) <!-- check: the slide link ends with "##/", probably a typo for "#/" -->
- [viz-js](http://viz-js.com/)
- [nomnoml](https://www.nomnoml.com/)

But [many more alternatives can be used](https://modeling-languages.com/text-uml-tools-complete-list/).

### The DOT language {#sec-l02-dot}

It is easy to start by following these rules:

- Variable names must not include space between words <!-- check: the rule says that names must not include spaces, but the slide examples use quoted names with spaces such as "Predictor 1" -->
- Arrows are represented by the characters `-` and `>`

What you type:

```{.dot}
digraph {
  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

What you get is shown in @fig-l02-dot-basic.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-dot-basic
//| fig-cap: "The diagram drawn by the first DOT code."
//| fig-alt: "Two ovals, Predictor 1 and Predictor 2, each with an arrow pointing down to an oval labelled Outcome."
//| fig-width: 2.84
//| fig-height: 1.37

digraph {
  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

To modify the orientation and the shape of the box, add the following options:

```{.dot}
digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

The result is shown in @fig-l02-dot-options.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-dot-options
//| fig-cap: "The diagram drawn with the options for the orientation and the shape of the boxes."
//| fig-alt: "Two boxes, Predictor 1 and Predictor 2, each with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Outcome on the right."
//| fig-width: 2.23
//| fig-height: 1.16

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

Unfortunately the way to plot an interaction is much trickier. You have to include an invisible box to design the arrow crossing the main arrow:

```{.dot}
digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Predictor 1"; "Predictor 2"; "Outcome"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Predictor 2" -> ""
  "Predictor 1" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> Outcome

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Predictor 2"; "";
  }
}
```

The result is shown in @fig-l02-dot-interaction.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-dot-interaction
//| fig-cap: "An interaction effect drawn with an invisible box."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Predictor 1 and a box labelled Outcome joined by a horizontal line with an arrowhead at Outcome. A box labelled Predictor 2 has an arrow pointing down to the middle of that line."
//| fig-width: 3.58
//| fig-height: 0.94

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Predictor 1"; "Predictor 2"; "Outcome"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Predictor 2" -> ""
  "Predictor 1" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> Outcome

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Predictor 2"; "";
  }
}
```

There are many more rules to make more complicated models, see for more details <https://graphviz.org/doc/info/lang.html>.

**DotUML extension for Google Docs.** This DOT language can easily be implemented with the DotUML extension in Google Docs. DotUML is developed by a company called BML Solutions but as far as I know it is a free plug-in (at least free of money). See <https://dotuml.com> for more details. After installing the extension, use GraphViz and remove the code corresponding to the default example.

::: {.callout-tip title="Your turn: draw the model(s) of your paper"}
In the research paper you have selected, **draw the model(s) tested.**

Remember, there is only 1 outcome variable per model and it is not possible to draw two models with the same outcome variable.

## Understanding the equation used to test hypotheses {#sec-l02-equations}

### A basic equation {#sec-l02-basic}

```{r}
#| label: l02-perfect-data
df <-
  data.frame(
    Observation = letters[1:11],
    Outcome = 10:0,
    Predictor = 10:0
  )
```

Let's imagine the perfect scenario: **your predictor variable explains perfectly the outcome variable**.

The corresponding equation is: $Outcome = Predictor$. @tbl-l02-perfect gives the data of this scenario and @fig-l02-perfect plots them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l02-perfect
#| tbl-cap: "Data of the perfect scenario."
gt(df) |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  opt_row_striping()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-perfect
#| fig-cap: "The perfect scenario: all the observations are on the prediction line."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the outcome against the predictor, both from 0 to 10. The 11 points lie exactly on a straight line rising from the bottom left to the top right."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
df |>
  ggplot(aes(Predictor, Outcome, label = Observation)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,10)) +
  theme_bw()
```

In the equation $Outcome = Predictor$, **three coefficients are hidden** because they are unused:

- the **intercept coefficient** $b_{0}$ (i.e., the value of the Outcome when the Predictor = 0) which is 0 in our case
- the **estimate coefficient** $b_{1}$ (i.e., how much the Outcome increases when the Predictor increases by 1) which is 1 in our case
- the **error coefficient** $e$ (i.e., how far from the prediction line the values of the Outcome are) which is 0 in our case

So in general, the relation between a predictor and an outcome can be written as:

$$Outcome = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Predictor + e$$ {#eq-l02-basic}

which is in our case:

$$Outcome = 0 + 1 * Predictor + 0$$

@eq-l02-basic is the same as the good old $y = ax + b$ (here ordered as $y = b + ax$) where $b_{0}$ is $b$ and $b_{1}$ is $a$. @fig-l02-b0-b1 shows the intercept and the estimate on the prediction line.

<!-- check: in the code below seq(0:10) returns 1 to 11, so the axis breaks start at 1 and not at 0 (seq(0, 10) was probably intended), and the size argument of geom_hline() is deprecated since ggplot2 3.4.0 (linewidth is the current one); the plot is unchanged -->

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-b0-b1
#| fig-cap: "The intercept b0 and the estimate b1 on the prediction line."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the outcome against the predictor, with 11 points on a rising straight line. A dotted horizontal line at 0 is labelled Intercept b0. A red step of one unit to the right and one unit up, along the line, is labelled Estimate b1."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
data.frame(Predictor = 0:10, Outcome = 0:10) |>
  ggplot(aes(Predictor, Outcome)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "black", size = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 0.2, label = "Intercept b0") +
  annotate("segment", x = 5, xend = 6, y = 5, yend = 5, color = "red") +
  annotate("segment", x = 6, xend = 6, y = 5, yend = 6, color = "red") +
  annotate("text", x = 7.5, y = 5.5, label = "Estimate b1") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0:10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0:10)) +
  theme_bw()
```

It is very important to know that under **EVERY** statistical test, a similar equation is used (t-test, ANOVA, Chi-square are all linear regressions). <!-- check: the Chi-square test is usually described as a log-linear model rather than a linear regression -->

### Relationship between variables {#sec-l02-relationship}

The relationship between a $Predictor$ and an $Outcome$ variable (stated in a main effect hypothesis or in an interaction effect hypothesis) is analysed in terms of: **"How many units of the Outcome variable increases/decreases/changes when the Predictor increases by 1 unit?"**

For example:

> How much Job Satisfaction increases when the Salary increases by €1?

The value of how much of the Outcome variable changes is called the **estimate** (also called the unstandardised estimate). It uses the letter $b$ in equations (e.g., $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, ...). For example:

> If Job Satisfaction increases by 0.1 on a scale from 0 to 5 when the Salary increases by €1, then *b* associated to Salary is 0.1

To evaluate if the strength of the relationship $b$ between a predictor and an outcome variable is significant, an equation is statistically tested using all the predictors related to the same outcome. The basic equation of a statistical model is:

$$Outcome = b_0 + b_n \,Predictors + Error$$

where the $Predictors$ includes all the $n$ variables used as predictor in formulated hypotheses using this specific $Outcome$ variable and being associated to a specific $b$ estimate. This expresses the idea that the outcome can be described by one or multiple predictors, and that the remaining part of the outcome's variability that is not explained by the predictors is called the error.

### Equations, variables and effect types {#sec-l02-effect-types}

Except in special cases:

- an outcome (or dependent variable) has to be continuous
- a predictor can be continuous or categorical

For example:

$$Job\,Satisfaction = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Salary + b_{2}\,Origin + e$$

In this equation, $Salary$ is continuous with a main effect on $Job\,Satisfaction$ ($b_{1}$) and $Origin$ is categorical with a main effect on $Job\,Satisfaction$ ($b_{2}$).

An interaction effect is represented by multiplying the 2 predictors involved:

$$Job\,Satisfaction = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Salary + b_{2}\,Origin + b_{3}\,Salary*Origin + e$$

In this equation, $Salary$ is continuous with a main effect on $Job\,Satisfaction$ ($b_{1}$), $Origin$ is categorical with a main effect on $Job\,Satisfaction$ ($b_{2}$), and $Salary$ with $Origin$ have an interaction effect on $Job\,Satisfaction$ ($b_{3}$).

### The relevance of the intercept {#sec-l02-intercept}

To test hypotheses, only the $b$ values associated to predictors (independent variables) are important. The intercept is always included in an equation but its result is useless for hypothesis testing. Let's see why the intercept is always included but discarded most of the time.

Imagine we want to test the relationship between GDP per Capita and Life Expectancy of countries in the world. Let's compare a model without and a model with intercept:

- Without intercept: $Life\,Expectancy = b_{1}\,GDP\,per\,Capita + e$
- With intercept: $Life\,Expectancy = b_{0} + b_{1}\,GDP\,per\,Capita + e$

@fig-l02-intercept shows the original data (A), the model without intercept (B) and the model with intercept (C). If the intercept is not included, the intercept is zero and can lead to estimation errors.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-intercept
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy and GDP per capita of the countries of the world in 2007 (gapminder data): the original data (A), the model without intercept (B) and the model with intercept (C)."
#| fig-alt: "Three scatter plots of life expectancy against GDP per capita. Panel A shows the original data only. Panel B adds a fitted line forced through the origin. Panel C adds a fitted line with an intercept."
#| fig-height: 5.5
p1 <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(
    title = "A: Original Data",
    x = "GDP per Capita ($)",
    y = "Life Expectancy"
  )

p2 <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE, formula = "y ~ x + 0 ") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(
    title = "B: Model without intercept",
    x = "GDP per Capita ($)",
    y = "Life Expectancy"
  )

p3 <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE, formula = "y ~ x") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(
    title = "C: Model with intercept",
    x = "GDP per Capita ($)",
    y = "Life Expectancy"
  )

p1 / (p2 + p3)
```

### Notes on the notation of equations {#sec-l02-notation}

Equations are not always written in the same way. Here are four notes on the notation.

1. **Greek or Latin alphabet?**

   $$Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\,X_{1} + \epsilon \; vs. \; Y = b_{0} + b_{1}\,X_{1} + e$$

2. **Subscript $i$ or not?**

   $$Y = b_{0} + b_{1}\,X_{1} + e \; vs. \; Y_{i} = b_{0} + b_{1}\,X_{1_{i}} + e_{i}$$

3. **Which sign between estimates and predictors?**

   $$Y = b_{0} + b_{1}.X_{1} + b_{2}*X_{2} + b_{3}\,X_{3} + e$$

4. **Hat on $Y$ or not? Capital letter or not?**

   $$\hat{Y}\; or\; \hat{y}\; vs.\; Y\; or\; y$$

### Representing an equation {#sec-l02-repr-eq}

Exactly like with models, there are different ways to communicate an equation in academic research outputs.

The least sophisticated approach would be to type the equation in Microsoft Word and to apply some italics and subscript style a posteriori. While there is nothing wrong with this approach, note that Microsoft Word has a tool to insert equations (Insert > Equations), then a GUI will help you to design special characters in equations.

Now there is a better way, which is also more complicated. LaTeX is used for entire manuscripts with all the specific design requirements imposed by the style of academic journals. LaTeX is hell and we will see a specific approach to avoid it, but the LaTeX style for equations is the best. <!-- check: "we will see a specific approach to avoid it" refers to a later lecture that the slide does not name -->

Here are the most basic rules:

- Start with `\begin{equation}` and end with `\end{equation}`
- Space between words can be added with `\,`
- To subscript a number use the underscore sign `_`

For example:

```{.latex}
\begin{equation}
  Outcome = b_0 + b_1\,Predictor 1 + b_2\,Predictor 2 + e
\end{equation}
```

Is translated as:

$$Outcome = b_0 + b_1\,Predictor 1 + b_2\,Predictor 2 +e$$

**Auto-LaTeX Equations for Google Docs.** Another fantastic extension is available for Google Docs, called Auto-LaTeX Equations. Instead of using `\begin{equation}` and `\end{equation}`, use `$$` to open and close the equation. Then, click on "Render Equation", for the equation to be transformed in LaTeX style. Note that some websites can help to create the LaTeX code, see for example <https://latex.codecogs.com/eqneditor/editor.php>.

**quiver.** quiver is a modern, graphical editor for commutative and pasting diagrams, capable of rendering high-quality diagrams for screen viewing, and exporting to LaTeX via tikz-cd or Typst via fletcher. See <https://q.uiver.app/>.

### Practice: from results to model and equation {#sec-l02-practice}

::: {.callout-tip title="Your turn: from results to model and equation"}
I will show you some results. Using these results:

1. Identify the role of variables,
2. Formulate the tested hypotheses,
3. Draw the corresponding model, and
4. Translate it in an equation.

Two examples follow, each with its solution.
:::

```{r}
#| label: l02-ex1-data
df3 <- tibble(
  Participant = c("ppt1", "ppt2", "ppt3", "ppt4", "ppt5", "ppt6"),
  `Sleep Time` = c(9, 5, 8.5, 7, 6.5, 5.5),
  `Exam Results` = c(89, 64, 71, 77, 78, 69)
)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Your turn: Example 1"}
Using the results obtained, identify the role of variables, formulate the tested hypotheses, draw the corresponding model, and translate it in an equation. @tbl-l02-ex1 gives the data and @fig-l02-ex1 the visualisation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l02-ex1
#| tbl-cap: "Data of Example 1."
df3 |>
  gt()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-ex1
#| fig-cap: "Exam results according to sleep time for the six participants of Example 1."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of exam results against sleep time. Each of the six points is labelled with its participant, ppt1 to ppt6."
#| fig-height: 3.5
df3 |>
  ggplot(aes(`Sleep Time`, `Exam Results`, label = Participant)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  geom_text_repel() +
  theme_bw()
```

Suggested time: 5 minutes.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true"}
**Variables**

- Outcome = Exam Results (from 0 to 100)
- Predictor = Sleep Time (from 0 to Inf.)

**Alternative hypothesis**

- $H_a$: **Exam Results** *increases* when **Sleep Time** increases
- ($H_0$: **Exam Results** *stays the same* when **Sleep Time** increases)

**Model** (@fig-l02-ex1-model)

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-ex1-model
//| fig-cap: "The model of Example 1."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Sleep Time with an arrow labelled b1 pointing to a box labelled Exam Results."
//| fig-width: 2.73
//| fig-height: 0.52

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Sleep Time" -> "Exam Results" [label= b1]
}
```

**Equation**

$$Exam\,Results = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Sleep\,Time + e$$
:::

```{r}
#| label: l02-ex2-data
df4 <- tibble(
  Participant = c("ppt1", "ppt2", "ppt3", "ppt4", "ppt5", "ppt6"),
  `Sleep Time` = c(9, 5, 8.5, 7, 6.5, 5.5),
  Age = c(50, 60, 70, 20, 30, 40),
  `Exam Results` = c(89, 64, 71, 77, 52, 69),
  Age_c = c("experienced", "experienced", "experienced", "beginner", "beginner", "beginner")
)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Your turn: Example 2"}
Using the results obtained, identify the role of variables, formulate the tested hypotheses, draw the corresponding model, and translate it in an equation. @tbl-l02-ex2 gives the data and @fig-l02-ex2 the visualisation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l02-ex2
#| tbl-cap: "Data of Example 2."
df4 |>
  select(-Age) |>
  gt()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-ex2
#| fig-cap: "Exam results according to sleep time for the six participants of Example 2, by age category."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of exam results against sleep time with one straight line for each age category, beginner and experienced, drawn in two colours."
#| fig-height: 3.2
df4 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `Sleep Time`, y = `Exam Results`, color = Age_c)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Suggested time: 5 minutes.
:::

::::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true"}
**Variables**

- Outcome = Exam Results (from 0 to 100)
- Predictor 1 = Sleep Time (from 0 to Inf.)
- Predictor 2 = Age (experienced vs beginner)

**Alternative hypotheses**

- $H_{a_{1}}$: **Exam Results** *increases* when **Sleep Time** increases
- $H_{a_{2}}$: **Exam Results** of **experienced students** are *higher* than for **beginner students**
- $H_{a_{3}}$: The effect of **Sleep Time** on **Exam Results** is *higher* for **experienced** than for **beginner students**

**Model** (@fig-l02-ex2-model)

::: {#fig-l02-ex2-model}

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-ex2-model-classic
//| fig-cap: "Classic representation."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Sleep Time and a box labelled Exam Results joined by a horizontal line with an arrowhead at Exam Results. A box labelled Age has an arrow pointing down to the middle of that line."
//| fig-width: 3.63
//| fig-height: 0.94

digraph {
 graph [rankdir = LR]

 node [shape = box]
 "Sleep Time"; "Exam Results"; Age
 node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
 ""

 Age -> ""
 "Sleep Time" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
 ""-> "Exam Results"

 subgraph {
   rank = same; Age; "";
 }
}
```

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-ex2-model-effects
//| fig-cap: "Effects correspondence."
//| fig-alt: "Three boxes, Sleep Time, Age and Sleep Time * Age, each with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Exam Results. The arrows are labelled b1, b2 and b3 respectively."
//| fig-width: 3.17
//| fig-height: 1.79

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]

  node [shape = box]
  "Sleep Time"; "Exam Results"; Age; "Sleep Time * Age"

  Age -> "Exam Results" [label= b2]
  "Sleep Time" -> "Exam Results" [label= b1]
  "Sleep Time * Age" -> "Exam Results" [label= b3]

  }
```

The model of Example 2.
:::

**Equation**

$$Exam\,Results = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Sleep\,Time + b_{2}\,Age + b_{3}\,Sleep\,Time*Age + e$$
:::::

## Conclusion {#sec-l02-conclusion}

To summarise, follow these steps:

1. **Variables**
    - Identify the role and type of each of your variables.
2. **Hypotheses**
    - Formulate your alternative hypotheses by using the proposed templates (@sec-lecture-01).
    - Any other formulation, even if it makes sense, is not good practice (for example using the terms "has an impact", "is related to", "influences", ...).
    - An interaction hypothesis requires the formulation of the main effect hypothesis of each predictor involved.
3. **Model**
    - A model should represent all your hypotheses and only your hypotheses.
    - Draw only one model per outcome variable (except when doing SEM analyses).
    - Use the same names or acronyms as your hypotheses.
4. **Equation**
    - Formulate your equation(s) in every paper that you want to submit (if reviewers want to remove it, they will tell you).

::: {.callout-note title="Key points"}
- A model gives an overview of the predicted relationships between variables: every arrow is a tested hypothesis, every tested hypothesis is an arrow, and each model has only one outcome variable (except SEM models).
- A simple arrow is a main effect and a crossing arrow is an interaction effect. Squares are measured items and circles are latent variables.
- Prefer a simple model: it is the most powerful, easy to test and reliable. Including an interaction effect requires a significantly higher sample size.
- Draw models in black and white with line arrows, using Word, PowerPoint, flowchart software or DOT code.
- Under every statistical test a similar equation is used, $Outcome = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Predictor + e$, where $b_{0}$ is the intercept, $b_{1}$ is the estimate (the change of the outcome when the predictor increases by 1) and $e$ is the error.
- The intercept is always included in the equation but is useless for hypothesis testing; leaving it out forces it to zero and can lead to estimation errors.
:::
